opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it as two things happening at once. On one hand, Marble is a real product that people can use today. You can give it a text prompt, an image, a few images, and it'll generate a persistent 3D world that you can actually walk around in, edit, and export into the tools you already use. So right now we're seeing people in gaming, in VFX and film previs, in design and architecture, even folks doing robotics simulation, pick it up because it saves them a ton of time building environments that used to take weeks of manual work.

But on the other hand, for us it's very much a step along the way, not the destination. When we started World Labs, the core thesis was that spatial intelligence, the ability to perceive, reason about, generate, and interact with 3D worlds, is a fundamental capability that's kind of missing from today's AI systems. Language models are amazing, but they live in a one-dimensional world of tokens. And we as humans and animals, we evolved to understand a three-dimensional world that has physics, that has objects, that persists over time, that you can act in.

So Marble is sort of the first concrete expression of that. Generation is one piece of spatial intelligence, and it happens to be a piece that's useful enough to ship and get into people's hands. And getting it into people's hands matters a lot, because it gives us feedback about what actually works, what people need, where the models break. It keeps us honest.

Longer term, what we want is models that don't just generate a static world, but that understand it deeply. Worlds that are interactive, that respond to agents, where you can reason about geometry and physics and cause and effect. That's going to be important for creative tools, but also for things like robotics and embodied agents, where you need a model of the world to plan and act. So I'd say Marble is useful today on its own terms, and it's also the foundation we're building on toward these much more general world models.

r001.rationale: The response describes Marble as a useful product people can use today and as a foundation for building more general world models over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that Marble is sort of our first step along a much longer road. The long-term vision for World Labs is really about spatial intelligence, which is this idea that AI systems should be able to understand, generate, and reason about the 3D world in the same way that today's language models can understand and reason about text. And that's a very big, very ambitious goal, and it's not something you get to in one shot.

So Marble, as it exists today, is a world model that lets you generate explorable 3D environments from a text prompt or an image or a few images, and you get something out that you can actually walk around in, that's persistent, that has real geometry. And people are already finding it useful today for things like game development, VFX, virtual production, architecture, design, even just creative exploration. And honestly, that's really important to us. I think there's a temptation in AI research to say, we're working on the big long-term thing and we'll ship something useful in five years. But I think you learn a lot more by putting things in people's hands now and seeing what they actually do with it, what breaks, where the gaps are.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of the capabilities we need for the long-term vision are already showing up in what Marble does. Generating a world that's geometrically consistent, that you can move around in, that has a sense of space, scale, and persistence, those are foundational pieces. And then on top of that you start to layer in things like editing, like composing worlds together, like letting people iterate rather than just hitting generate and taking what you get. Each of those is something that's useful on its own today, but it's also a piece of the bigger puzzle.

And then if you zoom out even further, the reason spatial intelligence matters is that the physical world is where a lot of important things happen. Robotics, embodied agents, simulation, anything where a machine has to act in a space rather than just talk about it. Those systems need to be able to perceive and generate and reason about 3D environments, and we think world models are going to be a core building block there. So Marble today is a creative tool, but the technology underneath it is the same technology that we think ultimately gets you to machines that really understand the world they're in. That's how I see the two fitting together.

r001.rationale: The response describes Marble as a useful creative tool today and calls its current capabilities foundational pieces of World Labs’ longer-term spatial intelligence vision.

astra-6.text:
I think of Marble as a concrete first step toward spatial intelligence. Today, the value is pretty tangible: you can take an idea or an image and turn it into a 3D world that you can move around in. That’s useful for people making games, films, or other kinds of interactive experiences, because it makes creating a space much easier.

But the longer-term ambition is broader than generating environments. We want systems that understand the structure of a world, how things relate to each other, and what happens when you interact with them. Being able to generate a compelling space is one piece of that; being able to reason and act within it is another.

So I see those as connected. Marble gives people something useful today, and putting it in their hands helps us learn what capabilities actually matter as we work toward that broader vision.

r001.rationale: The response calls Marble a “concrete first step” with useful applications today and connects it to the broader future goal of systems that understand and act within worlds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Marble as a first step toward making worlds a medium that people can create and work with. Today, there’s an immediate use case: you can take an idea or an image and turn it into a 3D environment that you can explore. That’s useful for creative work, whether you’re thinking about games, filmmaking, or designing a space, because you can move from imagining something to actually being inside it.

The longer-term vision is broader than generating a compelling environment. We want AI systems that understand the spatial structure of the world—how things fit together, what happens when you move around, and eventually how you can interact with and change that world.

So I see those as connected goals. Building something useful today gives people a way to tell us what matters: where they need more control, where consistency breaks down, what kinds of interactions they want. And those needs push us toward deeper spatial intelligence. Marble is an early expression of that vision, and a way to learn what it will take to get there.

r001.rationale: The response presents Marble as a useful product today and describes that work as a first step that helps advance the longer-term goal of deeper spatial intelligence.
